newsitem.title: IRELAND: EU promises action on beef amid protests.
newsitem.headline: EU promises action on beef amid protests.

text.p: European Union Agriculture Ministers pledged emergency steps on Tuesday to rescue the beef market from the mad cow crisis as a farmers' protest spilled on to the steps of their conference hotel.

But the three-day meeting failed to make headway towards resolving Britain's refusal to carry out in full a cattle cull which was supposed to shore up an industry hit by stayaway consumers and falling cattle market prices.

EU Agriculture Commisioner Franz Fischler told a news conference that a ban on British beef exports would not be lifted until the London government enacted in full an agreement worked out at an EU summit in Florence in June.

"It's in the hands of the British government," Fischler told a news conference delayed and disrupted when hundreds of Irish farmers broke through police cordons and reached the steps of the ministers' hotel to chant anti-British slogans.

Britain has suspended the slaughter of up to 147,000 young cattle because new scientific evidence shows that it will not hasten the elimination of BSE. But it is slaughtering up to one million older animals, as the Florence agreement stipulated.

Fischler said he was prepared to study Britain's new data but said it was no excuse for the London government to go back on an agreement supposed to lift the blight of BSE from the beef industry across Europe.
British farm minister Douglas Hogg had come under attack from his European partners in Killarney for his government's decision to suspend the additional slaughter of young cattle.
But after the meeting Hogg played down suggestions of conflict and indicated Britain would not adopt a policy of confrontation to make the situation even worse.
Hogg said the Florence agreement allowed for the discussion of scientific evidence. "We shall be working together with the commission and the scientific committees...", he said.

Cattle prices have fallen by up to 40 percent after Britain announced in March a link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and a fatal disease in humans. Beef consumption has dropped by an average 11 per cent in the EU.

Fischler announced plans to buy into storage around another 100,000 tonnes of beef to take it off a depressed market and try to brake the fall in prices paid to farmers. Some 400,000 tonnes has already been bought into the EU's storage.

Fischler said subsidies paid to livestock producers were being brought forward from next year to this year to provide cash for farmers. He gave no figures but EU officials said it was worth up to 500 million Ecus ($600 million).

"But for the action we have taken, the situation would have been much worse. The problem is the gulf between production and consumption which is over 20 per cent. It's a problem of consumer confidence," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates said.

Yates, whose country is current EU President, went out into the hotel car park to appeal with a megaphone to demonstrators to leave the area peacefully after a few small scuffles with police under driving rain.
The president of the Irish Farmers Association, John Donnelly, said it was too little and too late and accused Britain of sole responsibility for the crisis.
"We the Irish farmers are the innocent victims in the BSE crisis. It is a British problem and there was an agrement in Florence," he told reporters.

Several hundred demonstrators among 6,000 massed at the conference centre gates broke through police cordons and ran across fields when they realised that the three-day informal meeting would make no major breakthrough.
